cell-dev · evolved specimens · updated 2026-10-09

Spiking Tissue Atlas

Every body below grew from one cell. A genome decides how its cells divide and what each one becomes, and a grown cell only ever hears its immediate neighbours. Nobody wired an input or an output.

Part 1 is the newest work: bodies that chase a target across a screen during one continuous life, with no clock anywhere. Part 2 is the first task ladder, where flat bodies answered short timed trials. Pick a body: the replay starts mid-life, and “From the first cell” replays its growth from the zygote.

part 1 · BODY-1 pilot · 29 evolution runs · 2026-10-09

Bodies that steer a dot

The body is a dot on a screen, and its cells are stacked in layers. The bottom layer touches the screen: a cell there gets a receptor event now and then, more often when the target's halo is under it. A spike in the layer above twitches the dot outward on that cell's side. The middle cell of that layer clicks, and a click with the target inside the catch zone is a catch. Higher layers can only talk to the cells below them. Each cell fires when its own charge crosses threshold, and a spike takes about one time unit to reach a neighbour.

Score is catch income minus the cost of living cells, spikes and wasted clicks, per time unit. The replays below are one typical life of each body (the life whose score is nearest the median of 24), replayed in the reference simulator and checked against the fast one bit for bit.

Try it: place targets

Pick a body and give it something to chase. The cells below run on the same simulator as the replays, event by event, while you watch.

  • Tap or click an empty spot on the screen to drop a target. Up to six can be out at once.
  • Drag a target to move it. Double-tap it, or tap its ×, to take it away.
  • The body cannot see. A target only makes receptor events more frequent in the bottom-layer cells under its glow. When the centre cell clicks with a target inside the dashed circle, that target is caught.

The playground needs JavaScript to run the simulator.

what comes next · roadmap of 2026-10-09

Where this goes next

Evolution found real local algorithms, but not yet one that passes signals across the body better than a hand-built reflex, and hidden layers stay idle. Three studies followed the pilot: what limited it, how the cell logic could run on hardware, and which other kinds of cell would learn faster. Together they point to the plan below. The full roadmap, with costs and decisions, is docs/ROADMAP.md.

The questions worth answering

  1. What blocks signals that travel across the body: the search, the cell's building blocks, or a world that never rewards it?
  2. Can a body learn something while small and keep it as it grows?
  3. Which worlds give hidden layers, memory and adaptation a job?
  4. Do bodies cope with situations they were never trained on?
  5. Is this kind of cell the right one, or does a learning or logic-gate cell get further, faster?
  6. Can an evolved body run natively on a chip in real time?
first · days · $0

Fix the harness

Random tie-breaking (a bug froze four runs for 250+ generations), resume after interruption, an exact 1.24–1.35× faster kernel mode, new read-outs, and a map of which world settings reward computation.

first · 3 weeks · ≤ $150

Spike-bit tissue

Cells become small logic circuits that exchange spike bits, grow and divide. A neural cell trained by gradient on one GPU teaches them, then gets compiled into gates. What runs is the circuit, so it maps onto a chip as is. Milestones: grow and regrow, chase, regrow after losing half the body, learn around a mid-life motor flip.

alongside · about $10

What limited evolution

Continue the four best runs to 1,000 generations, seed a run with the hand-built router to see if selection keeps it, compare 4× more lives per genome, and test evolution strategies against the current algorithm. Also: can spike-timing learning replace the chemistry every body used for direction?

after week 3 · $15–45

Richer building blocks

Faster messages, a cleanup of the rules, gene duplication, and weights that depend on which face a spike arrives through. A 20-seed comparison, judged on counts of routers and mechanisms.

after the world map

Worlds that demand more

A different world drawn for each life, worlds that change mid-life, wounds that remove cells, and targets that blink out or must be intercepted, so memory, prediction and regrowth pay. Later: following a mouse cursor, reading a text stream.

later · months

Cells in silicon

An integer version of the model as the reference, then one cell processor, then a 37-cell array on a rented FPGA running a body in real time, then one cell on a shared chip run. Integer arithmetic already proved fitness-neutral on all 11 pilot bests.

What we can hope to see

  • The first body that beats the hand-built reflex by passing signals across itself, with a readable account of how.
  • A body that learns during its life: after its motors flip, its catches recover.
  • Regeneration: a body that loses half its cells, regrows and catches again.
  • Hidden layers that matter, once a world needs memory.
  • An evolved body running bit for bit on an FPGA, with measured gates and energy per cell.

Flat bodies answering timed trials

An earlier model on a flat grid with a global tick. Each organism grew, then faced short trials: grown cells react to light where they sit and pass spikes to their neighbours, and the score depends only on where in the body the firing ends up. Press play to watch a body grow, then work through a trial. Switch messages off to see what the cells can do alone. The red overlay marks the cells it cannot do without.
